Hello,

recently I have been experimenting with formalising planar graphs and I wanted to discuss my efforts with you all. The file is here. I will be glad for any opinions! I apologise in advance for the long post, but I wanted to write down my thoughts somewhere.

Of course, I am well aware that there has been a lot of discussion on how exactly to do this, and that the right framework to work with are multigraphs. Also, I know that there is an open PR on this topic (#16074). Nevertheless, I have decided to have my own go at it, and focus only on simple graphs since there is already a lot developed for them. My main goal was to build an environment where working with planarity would be as practical as possible.

I have decided to work with rotation systems instead of combinatorial maps because it seemed that defining a rotation system for a given graph would be easier than proving isomorphisms to a combinatorial map. The definition is as follows:

variable {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V)

/-- The set of the darts going out of a vertex. -/
def outDartSet (v : V) : Set G.Dart := {d | d.fst = v}

structure RotationSystem where
  rotation : Equiv.Perm G.Dart
  /-- For each vertex, the rotation is a cycle on the darts going out of it. -/
  isCycleOn_rotation (v : V) : rotation.IsCycleOn (G.outDartSet v)

(proving equivalence with #16074 should not be too difficult)

The faces can be elegantly defined as in the mentioned PR as the cycles of the face-rotation:

/-- The involution which reverses each dart. -/
def dartSymmPerm : Equiv.Perm G.Dart := Dart.symm_involutive.toPerm (α := G.Dart)

variable {G} (R : G.RotationSystem)

def faceRotation : Equiv.Perm G.Dart := R.rotation⁻¹ * G.dartSymmPerm

abbrev Boundary := Quot R.faceRotation.SameCycle

(Note that for disconnected graphs, this describes the facial boundaries, not faces themselves. Also, isolated vertices are ignored as there are no darts going out of them).

Of course, this is rather abstract to work with. I have therefore decided to think of the facial boundaries as sets of darts instead (mirroring the way support of a connected component is defined), and use the fact that the face-rotation is a cycle on them:

def boundaryMk (d : G.Dart) : R.Boundary :=
  Quot.mk _ d

/-- The set of the darts making up a facial boundary. -/
def supp {R : G.RotationSystem} (B : R.Boundary) : Set G.Dart := {d | R.boundaryMk d = B}

/-- The set of the boundaries of the rotation system, represented by their supports. -/
def boundarySet : Set (Set G.Dart) :=
  {F | F.Nonempty ∧ R.faceRotation.IsCycleOn F}

lemma ncard_boundarySet [Fintype R.Boundary] :
    R.boundarySet.ncard = Fintype.card R.Boundary := ...

Finally, we define planarity via Euler's formula (adjusted to reflect our definition of boundaries). I still did it via Boundary instead of boundarySet because it seemed more clean (and I could provide a computable Fintype instance, but I don't know whether there is any benefit to it):

def IsPlanar [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableRel G.Adj]
: Prop :=
  2 * Fintype.card V + Fintype.card R.Boundary =
    G.support.toFinset.card + G.edgeFinset.card + 2 * Fintype.card G.ConnectedComponent

variable (G)

def IsPlanar [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableRel G.Adj] : Prop := ∃ R : G.RotationSystem, R.IsPlanar

I then went on to prove the simplest result that I could think of: the disjoint union of planar graphs is planar.

Instead of using graph sum, I opted to work with Subgraph. In my opinion, this is the most natural since it allows us to consider the characteristics of the two graphs (vertices, edges...) "on the same level", in the underlying graph – which means that notions such as union, sharing vertices, deleting vertices are easy to state and study.

However, I had defined rotation systems only for graphs, and it would always be necessary to transfer the dart permutations. Therefore, I made the decision to remake everything again in the Subgraph API. For rotations, we simply extend them by identity elsewhere, making them a permutation on all darts of the underlying graph (this is for the sake of convenience so that they can be easily composed):

variable {G} (H : G.Subgraph)

/-- The set of the darts of the subgraph. -/
def dartSet : Set G.Dart := {d | H.Adj d.fst d.snd}

/-- The set of the darts going out of a vertex. -/
def outDartSet (v : V) : Set G.Dart := {d | H.Adj d.fst d.snd ∧ d.fst = v}

structure RotationSystem where
  rotation : Equiv.Perm G.Dart
  /-- For each vertex of the subgraph, the rotation is a cycle on the subgraph's darts
    going out of it. -/
  isCycleOn_rotation {v : V} (hv : v ∈ H.verts) : rotation.IsCycleOn (H.outDartSet v)
  /-- The rotation fixes all the darts not in the subgraph. -/
  eqOn_rest_rotation_one : H.dartSetᶜ.EqOn rotation (1 : Equiv.Perm G.Dart)

Planarity may simply be defined in terms of the corresponding rotation system of the subgraph's coercion to a graph; this is equivalent to planarity of the coercion:

def coe : H.coe.RotationSystem where ...

def IsPlanar (R : H.RotationSystem) [DecidableEq V] [Fintype H.verts] [DecidableRel H.Adj] : Prop :=
  2 * H.verts.toFinset.card + Fintype.card R.coe.Boundary =
    H.support.toFinset.card +  H.edgeSet.toFinset.card + 2 * Fintype.card H.coe.ConnectedComponent

def IsPlanar [DecidableEq V] [Fintype H.verts] [DecidableRel H.Adj] : Prop :=
  ∃ R : H.RotationSystem, R.IsPlanar

theorem coe_isPlanar [Fintype H.verts] [DecidableEq V] [DecidableRel H.Adj] :
    H.coe.IsPlanar ↔ H.IsPlanar := ...

The reason that we had to use the coercion is that the same definition of boundaries does not really work. However, this does not matter as in practice, we want to work with their supports anyway. Hence we may simply prove a set characterisation as before:

/-- The involution which reverses each dart of the subgraph and fixes the other darts. -/
def dartSetSymmPerm [DecidableRel H.Adj] : Equiv.Perm G.Dart :=
  H.coe.dartSymmPerm.extendDomain H.coeDartEquiv

variable {H} [DecidableRel H.Adj] (R : H.RotationSystem)

/-- The face-rotation of the subgraph rotation system; it fixes all the darts not in the
  subgraph. -/
def faceRotation : Equiv.Perm G.Dart :=
  R.rotation⁻¹ * H.dartSetSymmPerm

/-- The set of the boundaries of the rotation system, represented by their supports. -/
def boundarySet : Set (Set G.Dart) :=
  {F | F.Nonempty ∧ F ⊆ H.dartSet ∧ R.faceRotation.IsCycleOn F}

lemma ncard_boundarySet [Fintype R.coe.Boundary] :
    R.boundarySet.ncard = Fintype.card R.coe.Boundary := ...

Now we can finally prove our theorem; thanks to the definition, we simply use the composition of the two rotations!

variable {R} [DecidableEq V]  {G₁ G₂ : G.Subgraph}
variable [Fintype G₁.verts] [Fintype G₂.verts] [DecidableRel G₁.Adj] [DecidableRel G₂.Adj]

theorem isPlanar_disj_union (hdisj : Disjoint G₁.verts G₂.verts)
    (h₁ : G₁.IsPlanar) (h₂ : G₂.IsPlanar) : (G₁ ⊔ G₂).IsPlanar := ...

... well, almost. There are a few things I skipped over which should probably be their own posts.

First, I had to prove some lemmas about permutations, especially the IsCycleOn predicate. Over the course of doing so, I found the following useful restatement of Set.BijOn for permutations which might have merit as a separate definition (I am not sure if this had been done before). It may also be used as an argument to Equiv.Perm.subtypePerm:

/-- The proposition that a permutation fixes a set.  -/
def InvariantSet {α : Type u} (f : Equiv.Perm α) (s : Set α) : Prop :=
  ∀ ⦃x : α⦄, f x ∈ s ↔ x ∈ s

Second, and more importantly, the definition of planarity depends on the number of connected components, and I was a bit dissatisfied with relying on the coercion for subgraphs. In line with my philosophy of bringing everything to the same level, I transferred the theory of connected components to Subgraph. However, I am sure it could have been done in a better way; this was just an experiment to see if it would work well.

First, we can define walks for subgraphs, which are just like normal walks, but we impose the condition that the first vertex belong to the subgraph (to exclude nil walks on different vertices) and we only use adjacencies of the subgraph. Then we have a reachability relation for the whole underlying graph:

universe u
variable {V : Type u} {G : SimpleGraph V} (H : G.Subgraph)

inductive Walk : V → V → Type u
  | nil {u : V} (hu : u ∈ H.verts) : H.Walk u u
  | cons {u v w : V} (h : H.Adj u v) (p : H.Walk v w) : H.Walk u w
  deriving DecidableEq

def Reachable (u v : V) : Prop := Nonempty (H.Walk u v)

Now as with boundaries, components may be represented by their supports.

def componentSet : Set (Set V) :=
  Set.range ((Set.image (↑)) ∘ (ConnectedComponent.supp (G := H.coe)))

lemma ncard_componentSet [Fintype H.coe.ConnectedComponent] :
    H.componentSet.ncard = Fintype.card H.coe.ConnectedComponent := ...

And they are characterised by reachability in the subgraph, removing the need to refer to the coercion:

lemma mem_componentSet_eq {H : G.Subgraph} {v : V} {C : Set V} (hC : C ∈ H.componentSet)
    (hv : v ∈ C) : C = {u | H.Reachable v u} := ...

With everything set up, we may fill in the last missing piece:

variable {H} {G₁ G₂ : G.Subgraph}

theorem componentSet_disj_union (hdisj : Disjoint G₁.verts G₂.verts) :
    (G₁ ⊔ G₂).componentSet = G₁.componentSet ∪ G₂.componentSet ∧
      Disjoint G₁.componentSet G₂.componentSet := ...

Anyways, this is what I've done. In the future, I would like to prove that planarity is hereditary for subgraphs, and that the union of two planar graphs which share at most two vertices is planar. I believe given everything I have set up, it should be reasonably doable. Results like this would eventually be useful in proving the constructive part of Wagner's theorem.

If anyone has read this far, thank you and any comments/suggestions are welcome! I am still somewhat of a beginner, after all.

Hello! I have been working to prove Kuratowski's theorem with Graph. The "same level" is interesting because unlike SimpleGraph, using Graph you can talk about subgraphs and minors "on the same level". Unfortuantely, it is true that there isn't much about Graph in Mathlib just yet. We would welcome any contributions to it.

Interesting, I did not know that. I haven't really tried to work with Graph yet, but I may eventually do so. I think I will stick with SimpleGraph for now and see how far that goes – after all, once the groundwork is done, the next steps towards proving Kuratowski could be reasonably transferable. In any case, thanks for letting me know about your work (wow, you have done a lot!), I will take a look at it.
